The bigger story may be the reason employers give has flipped:

▪️ Market/economic conditions led for a 2nd straight month at 16,407 (37% of the month) and at 130,531 year to date has now overtaken AI as the top reason of 2026
▪️ AI cited for just 1,265 cuts in October, under 3% of the month and its lowest of the year — after peaking at 40% of May’s cuts and leading five straight months
▪️ Demand downturn 6,118 in the month, 21,347 year to date, +145%
▪️ Group every economic-weakness reason (market/economic conditions, closings, restructuring, contract loss, demand downturn, bankruptcy, financial loss) and you get 92% of October’s cuts and 66% year to date

Andy Challenger: “The reasons employers give have shifted from technology to the economy… That is a more cautious signal, though the overall pace of cutting remains low.”

▪️ Food led with 9,677, its highest month this year, 39,370 year to date +43%

▪️ Retail cut 3,692 in the same month it announced 13,300 hires

While there is no lack of interpretations of these relief rallies from a fundamental viewpoint, as usual, we approach them from a market structure perspective first. ...While the initial covering flows can provide a meaningful tailwind for equities, that source of mechanical demand is ultimately temporary. Once it has been exhausted, the market becomes increasingly sensitive to other sources of flow, which is essentially what we're left with today.

A couple of interesting posts in @C_Barraud's packed Thursday Brief indicate that while China’s stock rescue package got a shrug, as I posted on Tuesday, the US midterm results got a rally.

After Beijing rolled out its 2024-style support tools on Monday, the CSI 300 slipped 0.2% Tuesday and the tech-heavy Star 50 fell 3.8%. Then Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, and the CSI 300 jumped 2.3% Wednesday, its best day since July. It added 0.3% Thursday to 4,113, up 2.6% in two sessions.

Hong Kong followed with a bigger move Thursday:
▪️ The Hang Seng rose 3.7%, its best day since February 2025 (+4.0% on February 21, 2025, during the DeepSeek rally). It’s now up about 8% from its October 22 low.
▪️ The Hang Seng Tech rose 5.6%, the most since February 2025, per Bloomberg.
▪️ Alibaba and Tencent each rose more than 7%, and Meituan added 6.8%.

Investors are reading the result as a risk to the US AI hardware trade and rotating into value. China’s internet platforms are about as cheap as large-cap tech gets: Bloomberg notes the Hang Seng Tech traded at 13 times forward earnings last month, the lowest since 2024. Bloomberg Intelligence’s Marvin Chen sees three rotations at once. Money is moving out of Korea and Taiwan into China, into value after China was “stuck at trough valuations” while the rest of the world rallied, and away from “tech hardware and pure AI plays.”

The same rotation shows up in the US. Bespoke says 91.5% of consumer discretionary stocks are above their 50-day averages, the highest in at least a year, compared with 35.5% of tech stocks.

Positioning added fuel. Short selling was 32% of Hong Kong’s turnover on Tuesday, the highest in more than three years, according to Bloomberg. Lotus Asset Management’s Hao Hong calls the move “one of the biggest short squeezes in recent years.” The cost of hedging the Hang Seng Tech fell to its lowest since July, and options volume on the Tracker Fund hit a one-year high as bullish bets dominated.

To be fair to Beijing, Bloomberg also reported stepped-up national-team buying and buybacks Wednesday, so the policy floor is perhaps part of this. 

A caveat: Big up days aren’t reliable bottoms. Since 2000, the Hang Seng has had 53 separate days of 3.5% or more. While a month later it was higher 62% of the time (median +3.0%), three months later it was a coin flip: higher 53% of the time, with a median gain of 1.5%.

Bloomberg Economics has built a new inflation gauge, the Bloomberg Price Project, from millions of prices (web scrapes, card transactions, pharmacy data).

Its take: inflation is too high, but the drivers are narrow (oil and AI), which argues against urgent Fed hikes. Anna Wong, Bloomberg’s chief US economist and the lead author, expects the Fed to stay on hold through year-end.

▪️ Bloomberg Price Project headline 4.4% in September vs CPI 3.7%
▪️ But its trimmed mean (outliers cut across 30,000+ products) is 2.2% through October, vs the Cleveland Fed’s 2.7% and the Dallas Fed’s trimmed mean PCE at 2.3%
▪️ Rising: motor fuel +39.9% y/y, airfares +31.3%, software and memory +28.2%, laptops +57%
▪️ Falling: prescription drugs −7.3%, car insurance −5.5%
▪️ Groceries +2.9%, housing +3.1%; tariffs a one-time jump, not lasting inflation

Its key chart sorts every goods product into buckets by how fast its price is rising (below 0%, 0% to 5%, 5% to 10% and so on), weighted by how much households spend on each: 68% of goods spending saw price changes of 0% to 5% so far this year, vs 27% in 2022.

I ran the same exercise (12-month price changes weighted by share of spending) on BEA’s detailed PCE data (211 categories, goods and services):
